Thursday, 3 May 2029, morning. Hélène turns 87. She is very weak and no longer leaves her room. Ioana has come alone, with Rose-Hélène. Hélène wants to tell her, at last, about 3 May 1962.
Sit down, darling. I’d like to tell you something. I’ve never told anyone. Not even Odile.

Yes. It was a Thursday, like today. The weather was fine, very fine. The lime trees weren’t in flower yet, but the chestnut trees were. I was wearing a white dress my mother had sewn for my twentieth birthday.
That one. Henri was waiting for me in the park, on the bench, under the big lime tree. He looked nervous. He hadn’t slept: he had spent the whole night at the piano.
Yes. When I arrived, he stood up. He took a piece of paper out of his pocket and gave it to me. It was the score. I couldn’t read music, so he whistled it, right there on the bench, just for me.
Then he carved our initials into the tree with a little knife. And he kissed me. It was the first time. People were walking past, but we didn’t see them.
The next day he left for Algeria. He had received his call-up papers the week before, but he hadn’t told me. He wanted that day to be perfect.
Would you have preferred to know?
For sixty years I thought so. I could have told him I would wait for him. But today I think he was right. That day was perfect. It still is.
(strokes Rose-Hélène’s hair) Tell her one day. When she’s twenty. At the same time as you give her the waltz.

would have ("auriez préféré" = would have preferred)
time ("en même temps que" = at the same time as)
"Say-teh": the imperfect of "être". Both e’s are open.
"Noo vwa-yohn": the imperfect of "voir". "y" + "i" = a long "ee".
"A-dyuh": farewell for ever. More solemn than "au revoir".
In a story, the IMPERFECT describes the setting, the state of things, what usually happened or what was in progress. It’s the "background" against which the actions take place:
It was a Thursday. The weather was fine.
I was wearing a white dress.
Henri was waiting for me in the park. He looked nervous.
People were walking past, but we didn’t see them.
The PASSÉ COMPOSÉ expresses one-off actions that follow each other and move the story forward ("and then…"):
When I arrived, he stood up.
He took out a piece of paper and gave it to me.
He carved our initials. He kissed me.
Simple test: if you can ask "and then what happened?", it’s the passé composé. If it answers "what was it like?", it’s the imperfect.
3. The pluperfect: what had happened before
The PLUPERFECT (avoir / être in the imperfect + participle) shows an action EARLIER than the moment being told — a "flashback":
Il n’avait pas dormi. Il avait passé la nuit au piano.
Il avait reçu sa convocation la semaine d’avant.

Romanian uses the pluperfect ("scrisese", "primise") less and less and replaces it with the passé composé. French doesn’t: if an action comes before another one in the past, the pluperfect is required.
In novels, fairy tales and history books, the passé composé is replaced by the PASSÉ SIMPLE (ch. 36). You don’t need to use it, but you need to recognise it:
J’aurais pu lui dire que je l’attendrais.
Je resterai jusqu’à ce qu’elle s’endorme.
Il se peut qu’il pleuve. Il est probable qu’il fleurira.
C’était un jeudi. Il s’est levé. Il avait écrit une valse.
The unit’s sentence: "Avant qu’il ne parte, j’aurais dû lui dire que je l’attendrais ; il est probable qu’il serait revenu. Mais ce jour-là, il faisait beau, et il m’avait écrit une valse."

On Thursday 3 May 2029, Hélène turned eighty-seven. That day, Ioana and Julien were also celebrating two years of marriage. The weather was fine, just as it had been sixty-seven years before. In the care home garden, the chestnut trees were in flower, and the lime trees were just beginning to turn green.

Hélène hadn’t left her bed for a week. She had no fever, she wasn’t in pain anywhere. She was simply very tired, like someone who has made a very long journey. Dr Martin came to see her twice a day. She no longer said "one hour, not a minute more". She didn’t say much at all any more.

In the morning, Ioana had come alone with Rose-Hélène. Hélène had told her about 3 May 1962 for the first time: the bench, the white dress, the whistled waltz, the initials in the tree, the departure the next day. Ioana had listened without interrupting, holding her hand. When she left the room, she had cried for a long time in the corridor.

In the afternoon, the whole family came. Julien, Odile, Radu and Lucia, Karim and Leïla, Nathalie, and even Monsieur Garnier, Hélène’s nephew, who had come from Villefranche with a bunch of lily of the valley. Madame Lambert had made a cake. There was only one candle on it, shaped like a musical note.

Hélène could no longer blow. So it was Rose-Hélène who did it, sitting on the bed next to her, with Julien’s help. She blew so hard that she put out the candle and scattered half the icing sugar over the blanket. Hélène laughed. It was a small laugh, very weak, but it was her laugh.

Then Julien opened the window of the room. Downstairs, in the Salle Henri Bernard, Théo had sat down at the piano, with the windows wide open. He was fourteen now, and he played better and better. He played Henri’s waltz. The music rose up to the room, carried on the soft May air.

Hélène closed her eyes. She listened, a smile on her lips, very gently beating time with one finger on the sheet. When the waltz ended, Théo went straight on, without stopping, into Julien’s. The two waltzes, one after the other, like a single story. In the room, nobody spoke.

Before everyone left, Hélène asked Monsieur Garnier to give her a box that was in the drawer of her chest of drawers. Inside were several envelopes, one for each of them. She had been preparing them for weeks, in her small, shaky handwriting. She asked that they not be opened before the next day.

There was an envelope for Radu, one for Lucia, one for Odile, one for Madame Lambert, and even one for Yanis and one for Inès. There was a thicker one, addressed to "Julien and Ioana". And one last, tiny one, on which she had written: "For Rose-Hélène, for her twentieth birthday".

Around seven, the visitors left one by one. Each of them kissed her, each of them said "see you tomorrow". Hélène answered each with a smile. When it was Julien’s turn, she held on to his hand a moment longer. "Thank you," she murmured. "For the waltz. For everything."

Odile stayed. She had decided to spend the night there, in the armchair, as during the nights of fever. She switched off the big lamp and left only the little night light on the bedside table, next to the 1962 photo, Henri’s letter, the sprig of orange blossom and the photo of the foundation stone.

Around ten, Hélène opened her eyes. She looked at Odile for a long moment. Then she said, in a very weak voice: "Odile, will you do something for me? Will you whistle the waltz? The way he did, every 3 May. You heard it for forty years. I only ever heard him whistle it on the first day."

Odile hesitated. She had never whistled in front of anyone. Then she leaned towards the bed, took Hélène’s hand in hers, and began to whistle. Softly, a little out of tune at first, then more and more in tune. Henri’s waltz, just as he used to whistle it every year, in their kitchen in Marseille, while making the coffee.

Hélène smiled. She closed her eyes. When Odile finished, she heard Hélène murmur something. She leaned closer to hear. "He’s come back," said Hélène, very softly. Then she fell asleep, her hand in Odile’s, with the same smile as in the 1962 photo.

She didn’t wake up. At dawn, when the nurse came in, she found Odile asleep in the armchair, still holding Hélène’s hand. Hélène had passed away in the night, peacefully, without a sound, on the very day of her eighty-seventh birthday. As if she had waited for this 3rd of May to go.

It was Odile who called Julien, at six in the morning. She couldn’t say much. She only said: "She’s gone. She was smiling." Julien woke Ioana. They sat for a long time on the edge of the bed, in the dark, without speaking, holding hands. In the next room, Rose-Hélène was asleep.

They opened the "Julien and Ioana" envelope that morning, at the kitchen table, in front of two cups of tea they never drank. Inside was a long letter, and an official document signed at a notary’s. Hélène had left all her savings to the Conservatoire, to create a grant for the children of La Duchère.

She had wanted the grant to bear two names: "The Henri and Hélène Grant". In the letter, she explained that she had never had children, but that she had found thirty-six all at once, in the year she turned eighty-six. And that she wanted the most gifted to be able to carry on with music, even if their parents had no money.

The farewell ceremony took place the following Friday, in the Salle Henri Bernard. Hélène had asked for it in her letter: no church, no sad speeches, only music. The room was full. The residents in the front row, in wheelchairs, Madame Roux and Madame Lambert side by side, Monsieur Petit with his notebook.

Everyone Hélène had known in the last three years was there. The children of La Duchère, with their instruments. Their parents. The mayor. Claire Vasseur and Olivier Marchand, who had come from Paris. Monsieur Fournier, with a sprig from the old lime tree. Mihaela, with her țambal. Monsieur Mansouri, with his oud.

On a screen, on a video call from Iași, were the grandmother, Elena and Dan. The grandmother was wearing her finest ie. She was holding the embroidered tablecloth, the one with the bench and the lime tree and the two words: "Dor" and "Merci". She didn’t speak. She was crying silently.

Odile read the letter Hélène had left for everyone. Her voice trembled, but she read it to the end. At the last sentence, "And every 3 May, play the waltz. Not to cry. To dance", she looked up at the room. No one was holding back their tears any more.

Then the La Duchère orchestra played. Inès with Lucien’s clarinet, Yanis with the red-wood cello, the little ones with their buckets. They played "The Foundation Stone", then Henri’s waltz, arranged by Julien for the whole orchestra. Mihaela accompanied on the țambal. Monsieur Mansouri on the oud. Lucia on the guitar.

And in the middle of the waltz, something unexpected happened. Madame Lambert got up from her armchair and held out her hand to Monsieur Petit. Monsieur Petit took it. And they began to dance, slowly, between the rows, to the sound of the waltz. Then Odile took Julien’s hand. Then Ioana took Radu’s.

Within a few minutes, the whole room was dancing. Parents with children, residents with their families, the mayor with Claire Vasseur. Rose-Hélène was spinning round in the middle of the room, laughing, without knowing why everyone was crying and smiling at the same time. On the screen, in Iași, the grandmother had stood up and was dancing too, with Dan.

It wasn’t a sad ceremony. It was exactly what Hélène had asked for. A waltz. Children. Wrong notes. And people dancing instead of crying. When the music stopped, Olivier Marchand said quietly to Julien: "In forty years in music, I’ve never heard an orchestra play like that."

The following weeks were hard. On Wednesdays, Julien still took the funicular out of habit, then remembered, halfway up, that there was no one left to visit. He got off at Fourvière anyway, went to see Madame Lambert and Monsieur Petit, and played the waltz in the Salle Henri Bernard for the residents.

Odile was better. She had opened her own envelope the day after 3 May. She never told anyone what was inside. But since then, every morning, while making her coffee, she whistled the waltz. Victor, the cat, would sit next to her and listen, his eyes half closed.

On Saturday 14 June, at eight in the morning, Radu’s phone rang. It was Yanis. He was so excited he was talking too fast for anyone to understand. Radu had to ask him to repeat it three times. Then he understood. He hung up, woke Lucia, and called Ioana. "Come. Right now. To La Duchère."

An hour later they were all in front of the site: Radu, Lucia, Ioana, Julien with Rose-Hélène on his shoulders, Odile, and Yanis with his red watering can. The walls of the room were beginning to go up, in pale wood. In front of the entrance, the new bench had been installed the day before. And next to the bench was the young lime tree.

It had flowered. Not much. Just a few small clusters of pale yellow flowers, hidden under the leaves. Monsieur Fournier had said it probably wouldn’t flower until the following year. He had been wrong. The little lime tree had flowered in its very first summer, as if it hadn’t wanted to wait.

They all sat down together on the bench, squeezed up against each other. The air smelled of lime blossom, that sweet June scent everyone knows. Nobody said anything. Rose-Hélène climbed down from her father’s shoulders, went up to the tree, and touched a flower with the tip of her finger, very delicately, as Hélène had done on 15 April.

Then Odile began to whistle. Softly. Henri’s waltz. Julien smiled and began to whistle with her. Then Ioana. Then Radu, out of tune as always, and Lucia, laughing as she whistled. Yanis didn’t know the tune well enough, so he beat time on his watering can. And Rose-Hélène danced around the lime tree.

An old man walking down the street stopped to look at them: six adults on a new bench, whistling a waltz in the middle of a building site, a boy tapping on a watering can and a little girl spinning round a tree in flower. He shrugged, smiled, and went on his way, whistling too, without knowing why.

It was a Saturday in June. The weather was fine. The lime trees were in flower all over the city, and in the Parc de la Tête d’Or, on the bark of a very old tree by the lake, two H’s intertwined in a heart were waiting, as they had been waiting for sixty-seven years, for someone to come and sit in their shade.

After 3 May, Julien and Ioana find a letter from Hélène on the bedside table. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
My dear children, I call you that because that is what you have become. When you came into my life, three years ago, I was waiting. I didn’t even know what for any more.
You found a waltz in a piano. You could have thrown it away, or kept it in a drawer. You chose to find out whom it belonged to. And you found me.

Since then, I have danced at a wedding, taken a plane, learned the hora, watched a little girl take her first steps towards me. I have smelled Seville in a sprig of orange blossom. I have laid a foundation stone.
You will probably be sad when you read this letter. Don’t be sad for too long. I waited sixty years for Henri to come back. He didn’t come back. But you came in his place.

I have asked my nephew to give my savings to the Conservatoire, so that the children of La Duchère can carry on with music when they grow up. A small grant. Let it bear both our names: Henri and Hélène.
And every 3 May, play the waltz. Not to cry. To dance. With love to all three of you, and to all the others. Your Hélène.
are ("vous êtes devenus" = you have become)
has ("il y a trois ans" = three years ago)
place ("à sa place" = in his place)
